screens.title: Traffic Light, Vending Machine, and Line-Tracking Robot FSMs
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we build three practical finite state machines you can run on a microcontroller: a traffic light with a pedestrian override, a vending machine handling coins and selections, and a line-tracking robot driven by two infrared sensors. You will learn not only how to model states and transitions, but also a useful pattern: separate the decision logic that chooses the next state from the output logic that drives LEDs, motors, or displays. That separation makes code easier to read and to unit test. We'll also add simple UART trace output so you can observe state changes in real time and debug unexpected behavior. As you follow the examples, notice how inputs such as buttons or sensors override timers, and how missing transitions create stuck states. By the end you will be ready to implement these FSMs on a LaunchPad, add trace logging, and try a design challenge to extend a traffic light with a late-night blink mode. Think about where you would place timers, where interrupts might help, and what you would log to the UART to make debugging straightforward.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these sections you will be able to model and implement finite state machines for real embedded problems, map inputs and outputs to hardware, and use trace output for debugging. First, you'll implement a traffic light FSM that uses timers and an external button so that a pedestrian request immediately forces the sequence toward a safe stop. Second, you'll design a vending machine FSM that accepts coins, allows selection, dispenses items, and returns change while keeping state transitions explicit. Third, you'll apply FSM thinking to a line-tracking robot that reads two infrared sensors and reacts instantly to keep a vehicle on a path. Finally, you will add UART trace output so you can see the current state and inputs at runtime, which is essential for debugging asynchronous events. Each objective pairs a practical skill with a simple verification milestone so you can confirm competency on hardware or in simulation.

screens.title: Bloom Competencies
screens.narratorSegment: These activities follow a Bloom-like progression. First you will learn the core vocabulary and simple three-state patterns by reading code and watching the traffic light demo. Next you will understand how inputs such as a pedestrian button or sensors override timers and how that affects safety and responsiveness. Then you will apply the pattern by implementing a vending machine FSM that cleanly separates state transitions from output actions. Finally you will master the debugging workflow by adding UART trace output and using that log to find missing transitions or timing issues. Each step is practical: for example, applying means mapping LEDs and a push button on a LaunchPad and verifying that pressing the button triggers the walk phase. Mastery means you can explain a failing test using only the trace log and then fix the state logic. This structure keeps practice focused and verifiable.

screens.title: Traffic Light Controller — real requirements
screens.narratorSegment: A traffic light controller for a four-way intersection must do more than cycle green, yellow, and red. It must handle asynchronous inputs like a pedestrian button and emergency sensors, adjust timing for time of day, and ensure safety when inputs arrive during a transition. In this lesson we define the concrete requirements that drive our FSM design. The key states we will use are green, yellow, red, and a dedicated walk phase. The pedestrian button acts as an input that overrides a normal timer: when pressed it should cause the system to move towards yellow immediately so pedestrians can safely cross. Timers still matter: each state has a timeout that triggers the next state when time expires. A common misconception is to bake output actions directly into transition conditions; instead, separate the decision of the next state from the actions that drive LEDs. This separation prevents side-effects from making transitions hard to test. A practical verification is to press the pedestrian button during green and confirm that the UART trace shows a transition to yellow, then red, then walk. What input sequences could still lead to unsafe behavior if timers are too short?

keyIdea.title: Define requirements first
keyIdea.text: List states, inputs, timers, and safety overrides before writing transition code.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › Traffic Light Requirements
Essential elements
  • States: GREEN, YELLOW, RED, WALK with independent timers.
  • Inputs: pedestrian button, timer expiration, optional emergency sensor.
  • Behavior: pedestrian press forces transition toward YELLOW, then RED, then WALK.
  • Verification: UART prints state and input each cycle for debugging.
Key Takeaway

Safety and clear input priorities drive the FSM structure; define them before coding.

Concrete example
If the system is GREEN and the pedestrian button is pressed, set the next state to YELLOW and reset the green timer. Even if the timer was not yet expired, the override ensures pedestrians are served promptly.
Common mistake
Putting LED control into transition checks can hide side effects; centralize outputs so tests can simulate states without hardware toggles.

screens.title: Traffic Light FSM — code walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a compact C-style FSM that implements the traffic light with a pedestrian override. The state enum lists GREEN, YELLOW, RED, and WALK, and a single trafficLightFSM function runs each cycle. Inside that function a switch on the current state sets outputs and checks two kinds of inputs: a pedestrian button and a timerExpired flag for that state. Notice the pattern: the output actions — setting LEDs or clearing the walk LED — are visible in each case, but the actual state transition is only driven by simple conditions: either the pedestrian button or a timer expiration. A concrete example: when in GREEN, if the pedestrian button is true, we immediately set state to YELLOW and reset the green timer. A common misconception is expecting the timer variables to be the sole driver; in embedded systems, asynchronous inputs can and should override timers for safety. For testing add a trace function that prints the numeric state and a packed input mask to the UART every time the FSM runs. With that trace you can replay sequences and check that button presses cause the expected transition order.

keyIdea.title: Switch-based FSM pattern
keyIdea.text: Use an enum and a single dispatcher that reads inputs, decides next state, and keeps outputs separate for easier testing.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › Traffic Light Code
Core snippet
typedef enum { GREEN, YELLOW, RED, WALK } TrafficLightState;

TrafficLightState state = GREEN;

void trafficLightFSM(uint8_t pedestrianButton, uint8_t timerExpired) {
    switch (state) {
        case GREEN:
            setGreenLED(); clearWalkLED();
            if (pedestrianButton || timerExpired) { state = YELLOW; }
            break;
        case YELLOW:
            setYellowLED(); clearWalkLED();
            if (timerExpired) { state = RED; }
            break;
        case RED:
            setRedLED();
            if (timerExpired) { state = WALK; }
            break;
        case WALK:
            setWalkLED();
            if (timerExpired) { state = GREEN; }
            break;
        default:
            state = GREEN; break;
    }
}
Example: press the pedestrian button while GREEN; the state sequence becomes YELLOW → RED → WALK regardless of green timer remaining.
Explanation bullets
  • The enum gives readable state names for clarity and debugging.
  • The FSM runs repeatedly, checking inputs and timers each cycle.
  • Reset timers when you change state so durations are consistent.
  • Separate state selection from output side-effects to ease simulation.
Misconception: Timers alone are not sufficient; external inputs must be allowed to pre-empt timers for safety.

screens.title: Pedestrian Override & Timers
screens.narratorSegment: Timers and asynchronous inputs must work together cleanly. The usual pattern is to maintain per-state timers and, on a state change, reset the timer for the new state. When an external event like a pedestrian button is detected we treat it as a higher-priority input that forces the next state regardless of the remaining time in the current state. Concretely, when in GREEN and the pedestrian button is pressed, set the state to YELLOW and set the green timer to zero so the next cycles treat the yellow timer as the active countdown. This avoids ambiguous timer ownership across states. A clear example is a late press during YELLOW: if your code ignores the button there, pedestrians may never get a WALK phase; instead, have your priority rules documented. For robustness, consider debouncing the button and, if needed, use interrupts to signal the event and set a flag read by the FSM loop. A common mistake is to let the timer update and then trigger transitions in multiple places; keep timer logic local and explicit so it is easy to reason about safety and to write tests that simulate time advancing.

keyIdea.text: Reset per-state timers on entry and make external inputs higher-priority to ensure predictable safety transitions.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › Pedestrian Override
Step-by-step flow
1. Detect
Read button or interrupt flag and debounce to avoid false triggers.
2. Prioritize
Treat the event as higher priority than the normal timer if safety requires it.
3. Transition
Set next state and reset the appropriate timer on entry.
Example: A pedestrian press during GREEN sets state to YELLOW and resets greenTimer. That ensures yellowTimer governs the duration until RED and WALK.
Checks
  • Debounce physical switches to avoid multiple transitions.
  • Document priority rules so that multiple inputs do not conflict.
  • Simulate late inputs to verify WALK still occurs.
Common mistake

Failing to reset timers on state entry can create unexpected short or long phases.

screens.title: Vending Machine FSM — states and inputs
screens.narratorSegment: A vending machine is a canonical FSM example because it combines multiple inputs and outputs across several states. The states we use are Idle, AcceptingCoins, SelectionMade, Dispensing, and ReturningChange. Inputs include CoinInserted, ButtonPressed for selection, CancelPressed, and ItemDispensed from the dispenser sensor. Outputs are DisplayMessage, OpenDispenser, and ReturnCoins. The important conceptual separation is that the state logic decides the next state based on inputs, while the output logic decides what must be shown or activated in the current state. For example, in AcceptingCoins the machine accumulates credit until a ButtonPressed input produces SelectionMade if enough credit exists. A concrete test case: insert coins totaling the exact price, press the selection button, and verify the dispenser opens and the machine transitions to Dispensing then to Idle after ItemDispensed. A common misconception is to mix monetary accounting and hardware outputs into transition code; instead keep a simple state machine that updates a credit variable and a separate output handler that drives the display and actuator. This approach simplifies debugging and lets you simulate state transitions in software without hardware. Vending Machine FSM — states and inputs means list distinct states and map each to inputs and outputs; keep accounting separate from output actions.. In practical terms, map the classic vending-machine states to clear inputs and outputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › Vending Machine FSM
States
  • Idle — waiting for coins
  • AcceptingCoins — accumulate credit
  • SelectionMade — validate and prepare dispense
  • Dispensing — open dispenser until ItemDispensed
  • ReturningChange — issue coins when needed
Inputs & Outputs
Inputs: CoinInserted, ButtonPressed, CancelPressed, ItemDispensed.
Outputs: DisplayMessage, OpenDispenser, ReturnCoins.
Verification: run a simulated coin sequence and confirm the trace shows expected state transitions and output actions.

screens.title: State Logic vs Output Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Separating state decision logic from output logic is a design pattern that reduces coupling and makes both simulation and testing easier. State logic answers the question: given the current state and inputs, what is the next state? Output logic answers: given the current state, what hardware signals or display messages should be active? Consider a vending machine: a transition from AcceptingCoins to SelectionMade depends on sufficient credit and a selection input. The output logic then decides whether to show "Please wait", open the dispenser, or animate a change-return. If you mix outputs into transition checks, a unit test that simulates a transition might inadvertently attempt to toggle hardware. By separating them, you can test the state machine in isolation and then run a small output renderer to map states to hardware. A misconception is thinking this separation adds overhead; in practice, it simplifies reasoning and lets you add trace prints for state and inputs without spurious side effects. Example: test selection logic in software, then verify output mapping only when hardware is connected. State Logic vs Output Logic means keep state decision logic independent from output side-effects to simplify testing and reduce errors.. In practical terms, why separate state transitions from the outputs they trigger. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › State vs Output
State Logic
Decides next state using current state and inputs. No hardware toggles. Example: if credit >= price and ButtonPressed, nextState = DISPENSING.
Tests: run sequences of input events in software and assert expected state sequence.
Output Logic
Maps the current state to outputs that drive LEDs, motors, or displays. Example: if state == DISPENSING then OpenDispenser = true.
Benefit: you can run output logic only when hardware is attached, keeping the FSM portable.

screens.title: Vending Machine Assessment — find the missing transition
screens.narratorSegment: A common assessment is to present a vending machine state diagram that is almost complete but missing a single arrow. Your task is to identify the missing transition and explain the runtime consequence. For example, if there is no transition from Dispensing back to Idle when an ItemDispensed input arrives, the machine could remain stuck in Dispensing and never accept new coins. To approach this systematically, list each state and enumerate all inputs that can realistically occur while the machine is in that state. Ask: for each input, where should the machine go? If an input is not handled, simulate a trace that shows the FSM encountering that input and remaining in the same state; this reveals a stuck or unsafe condition. A concrete fix is to add a transition from Dispensing to Idle on ItemDispensed and ensure outputs are updated in the output logic. This exercise trains you to think in terms of exhaustively handling inputs per state and to use UART trace logs to confirm the missing transition in a live test. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › Find the Missing Arrow
Diagnostic steps
  1. List every input possible in the current state.
  2. For each input, define the intended next state.
  3. Simulate sequences and watch traces for unhandled inputs.
  4. Add transitions and test again on hardware or in simulation.
Example fix
Add: if (state == DISPENSING && ItemDispensed) state = IDLE; Also ensure the output logic closes the dispenser and updates the display.
Use the UART trace to confirm the ItemDispensed event and the subsequent state change in real tests.

screens.title: Line-Tracking Robot FSM
screens.narratorSegment: A line-tracking robot is a straightforward example of a reactive FSM. The robot uses two infrared sensors, left and right, to detect a dark line on a lighter surface. We define three states: MovingForward, TurningLeft, and TurningRight. The state transitions are simple: if both sensors read white, the robot moves forward; if the left sensor sees black it should turn left, and if the right sensor sees black it should turn right. This reactive pattern emphasizes immediate response to sensor inputs, not timed phases. A concrete example: while moving forward, when the left sensor detects black the FSM sets state to TurningLeft and output logic drives the left motor slower or reverses so the robot turns. A misconception is to add long timers to these transitions; instead transitions should be immediate and tuned for responsiveness. For testing, simulate sensor inputs and log the FSM state to the UART each cycle to verify that sensor sequences produce the expected turning behavior and that the robot returns to MovingForward once sensors realign. Line-Tracking Robot FSM means make sensor-driven state changes immediate and test using traces of sensor values and state.. In practical terms, three states driven by two infrared sensors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: UART Trace — observe state and input
screens.narratorSegment: Debugging an FSM on hardware requires being able to observe internal state. A practical and minimal solution is to add a trace function that prints the current state and a compact representation of the inputs to the UART every time the FSM runs. For example, a trace function can print a line like State: 2, Input: 0x03. This line gives you a step-by-step record of what the FSM saw and what it chose. When you press the pedestrian button, the trace will show the input change in the very next cycle and the following state transition. A common misconception is that traces slow the system too much; print sparsely or at a lower baud rate for long-term use, and use traces primarily during debugging. Another tip: include timestamps or cycle counters to correlate trace lines with physical events or a logic analyzer. Example code shows how to format the state and an input mask, and it is helpful to include human-readable state names in debug builds. End every debugging session by removing or gating traces to avoid filling flash or slowing critical loops.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.2 › UART Trace
Trace snippet
void traceFSM(uint32_t state, uint32_t input) {
    UART0_SendString("State: ");
    UART0_SendNumber(state);

screens.title: Add a 'Yellow Blink' Late-Night Mode
screens.narratorSegment: As a design challenge, add a new YellowBlink state to support late-night operation. The idea is that during low-traffic hours the light should blink yellow instead of cycling normally. To implement this, add a new enum value YELLOW_BLINK and a condition in your state-selection logic that enters this state when a time-of-day flag is set. Output logic in YELLOW_BLINK should toggle the yellow output on and off at a chosen blink interval. A concrete example: if timeOfDay == NIGHT and no pedestrians are requesting crossing, transition from GREEN to YELLOW_BLINK when the current cycle completes. Important considerations: ensure a pedestrian button still forces a safe transition out of blinking to the normal stop-and-walk sequence; in other words, the override rule should still apply. This challenge reinforces extending FSMs safely while preserving priority rules and testability. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we build three practical finite state machines you can run on a microcontroller: a traffic light with a pedestrian override, a vending machine handling coins and selections, and a line-tracking robot driven by two infrared sensors. You will learn not only how to model states and transitions, but also a useful pattern: separate the decision logic that chooses the next state from the output logic that drives LEDs, motors, or displays. That separation makes code easier to read and to unit test. We'll also add simple UART trace output so you can observe state changes in real time and debug unexpected behavior. As you follow the examples, notice how inputs such as buttons or sensors override timers, and how missing transitions create stuck states. By the end you will be ready to implement these FSMs on a LaunchPad, add trace logging, and try a design challenge to extend a traffic light with a late-night blink mode. Think about where you would place timers, where interrupts might help, and what you would log to the UART to make debugging straightforward.

By the end of these sections you will be able to model and implement finite state machines for real embedded problems, map inputs and outputs to hardware, and use trace output for debugging. First, you'll implement a traffic light FSM that uses timers and an external button so that a pedestrian request immediately forces the sequence toward a safe stop. Second, you'll design a vending machine FSM that accepts coins, allows selection, dispenses items, and returns change while keeping state transitions explicit. Third, you'll apply FSM thinking to a line-tracking robot that reads two infrared sensors and reacts instantly to keep a vehicle on a path. Finally, you will add UART trace output so you can see the current state and inputs at runtime, which is essential for debugging asynchronous events. Each objective pairs a practical skill with a simple verification milestone so you can confirm competency on hardware or in simulation.

These activities follow a Bloom-like progression. First you will learn the core vocabulary and simple three-state patterns by reading code and watching the traffic light demo. Next you will understand how inputs such as a pedestrian button or sensors override timers and how that affects safety and responsiveness. Then you will apply the pattern by implementing a vending machine FSM that cleanly separates state transitions from output actions. Finally you will master the debugging workflow by adding UART trace output and using that log to find missing transitions or timing issues. Each step is practical: for example, applying means mapping LEDs and a push button on a LaunchPad and verifying that pressing the button triggers the walk phase. Mastery means you can explain a failing test using only the trace log and then fix the state logic. This structure keeps practice focused and verifiable.

A traffic light controller for a four-way intersection must do more than cycle green, yellow, and red. It must handle asynchronous inputs like a pedestrian button and emergency sensors, adjust timing for time of day, and ensure safety when inputs arrive during a transition. In this lesson we define the concrete requirements that drive our FSM design. The key states we will use are green, yellow, red, and a dedicated walk phase. The pedestrian button acts as an input that overrides a normal timer: when pressed it should cause the system to move towards yellow immediately so pedestrians can safely cross. Timers still matter: each state has a timeout that triggers the next state when time expires. A common misconception is to bake output actions directly into transition conditions; instead, separate the decision of the next state from the actions that drive LEDs. This separation prevents side-effects from making transitions hard to test. A practical verification is to press the pedestrian button during green and confirm that the UART trace shows a transition to yellow, then red, then walk. What input sequences could still lead to unsafe behavior if timers are too short?

Let's walk through a compact C-style FSM that implements the traffic light with a pedestrian override. The state enum lists GREEN, YELLOW, RED, and WALK, and a single trafficLightFSM function runs each cycle. Inside that function a switch on the current state sets outputs and checks two kinds of inputs: a pedestrian button and a timerExpired flag for that state. Notice the pattern: the output actions — setting LEDs or clearing the walk LED — are visible in each case, but the actual state transition is only driven by simple conditions: either the pedestrian button or a timer expiration. A concrete example: when in GREEN, if the pedestrian button is true, we immediately set state to YELLOW and reset the green timer. A common misconception is expecting the timer variables to be the sole driver; in embedded systems, asynchronous inputs can and should override timers for safety. For testing add a trace function that prints the numeric state and a packed input mask to the UART every time the FSM runs. With that trace you can replay sequences and check that button presses cause the expected transition order.

Timers and asynchronous inputs must work together cleanly. The usual pattern is to maintain per-state timers and, on a state change, reset the timer for the new state. When an external event like a pedestrian button is detected we treat it as a higher-priority input that forces the next state regardless of the remaining time in the current state. Concretely, when in GREEN and the pedestrian button is pressed, set the state to YELLOW and set the green timer to zero so the next cycles treat the yellow timer as the active countdown. This avoids ambiguous timer ownership across states. A clear example is a late press during YELLOW: if your code ignores the button there, pedestrians may never get a WALK phase; instead, have your priority rules documented. For robustness, consider debouncing the button and, if needed, use interrupts to signal the event and set a flag read by the FSM loop. A common mistake is to let the timer update and then trigger transitions in multiple places; keep timer logic local and explicit so it is easy to reason about safety and to write tests that simulate time advancing.

A vending machine is a canonical FSM example because it combines multiple inputs and outputs across several states. The states we use are Idle, AcceptingCoins, SelectionMade, Dispensing, and ReturningChange. Inputs include CoinInserted, ButtonPressed for selection, CancelPressed, and ItemDispensed from the dispenser sensor. Outputs are DisplayMessage, OpenDispenser, and ReturnCoins. The important conceptual separation is that the state logic decides the next state based on inputs, while the output logic decides what must be shown or activated in the current state. For example, in AcceptingCoins the machine accumulates credit until a ButtonPressed input produces SelectionMade if enough credit exists. A concrete test case: insert coins totaling the exact price, press the selection button, and verify the dispenser opens and the machine transitions to Dispensing then to Idle after ItemDispensed. A common misconception is to mix monetary accounting and hardware outputs into transition code; instead keep a simple state machine that updates a credit variable and a separate output handler that drives the display and actuator. This approach simplifies debugging and lets you simulate state transitions in software without hardware. Vending Machine FSM — states and inputs means list distinct states and map each to inputs and outputs; keep accounting separate from output actions.. In practical terms, map the classic vending-machine states to clear inputs and outputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Separating state decision logic from output logic is a design pattern that reduces coupling and makes both simulation and testing easier. State logic answers the question: given the current state and inputs, what is the next state? Output logic answers: given the current state, what hardware signals or display messages should be active? Consider a vending machine: a transition from AcceptingCoins to SelectionMade depends on sufficient credit and a selection input. The output logic then decides whether to show "Please wait", open the dispenser, or animate a change-return. If you mix outputs into transition checks, a unit test that simulates a transition might inadvertently attempt to toggle hardware. By separating them, you can test the state machine in isolation and then run a small output renderer to map states to hardware. A misconception is thinking this separation adds overhead; in practice, it simplifies reasoning and lets you add trace prints for state and inputs without spurious side effects. A common assessment is to present a vending machine state diagram that is almost complete but missing a single arrow.
